lines.text: A wine cellar is a climate-controlled space designed for storing and ageing wine under optimal conditions. Temperature is the most critical factor — ideally between 11 and 14 degrees Celsius, constant and free from fluctuation. Humidity should be maintained at 60–70% to prevent corks from drying out and allowing air ingress, which spoils the wine. Bottles are stored horizontally on racks so the wine keeps the cork moist from the inside. Vibration must be minimised — underground cellars are ideal because they naturally dampen movement and maintain stable temperatures. Darkness is essential: ultraviolet light degrades wine, which is why most fine wines come in dark-coloured glass. A serious wine cellar is organised systematically — bins or racks labelled by region, grape variety, vintage, and drinking window. A cellar book or digital inventory tracks each bottle: its provenance (where purchased), price paid, drinking notes, and recommended maturity. 'Laying down' wine — buying young wines to age over years or decades — is both an investment and a passion for collectors. Some wines improve dramatically with age: tannins soften, flavours integrate, and secondary and tertiary characteristics develop. Others — most whites and lighter reds — are meant to be drunk young. Knowing which wines to cellar and when to open them is the hallmark of a knowledgeable collector.
